title: 12/03 — Academic term patterns (the three named literals, and the researched rest)
owner: P6 (injected) — Task 12's `DatePatterns` (the three named academic-term patterns are required members)
consumer: P6 Task 12 (src/facts/dates.py): `date_candidates(observation, *, patterns)` then `parse_exact(raw, *, pattern_id)`. Candidates fill the `term` field through §3.7's ranked fill-or-abstain. Also CONNECTION.md section 4 step 1: a term-pattern hit is a deterministic Academic activation signal (never alone — a term co-activates nothing by itself; see rules).
match_field: raw text of an observation in any text-bearing zone. The match is a candidate for the `term` field; parse_exact derives the normalized value from the named groups of the dedicated pattern — never from fuzzy parsing.
normalization_for_matching: per-entry case rule (see entries — season words tolerate case, designators like AY/WiSe do not). Word-boundary everywhere Latin script allows it; the CJK row uses lookarounds because CJK characters are word characters to the regex engine and `\b` cannot bound them.
evaluation_order: prefixed and worded patterns first (AY, WS, Wintersemester/Sommersemester, WiSe/SoSe, named terms, quarters, semesters), the standalone year-range family last. A span claimed by an earlier pattern is not offered to a later one — `AY 2024-25` is one AY candidate, never additionally a standalone `2024-25` candidate. Claiming crosses catalogues: 12/04's designator families run in the worded band too, so `FY 2024-25` is claimed by 12/04 `fam-fiscal-year` (a tax-year candidate, never a term) and is not offered to the standalone range rows here — the combined order is written once in 12/README.md. check.py enforces the in-file half by asserting each of the three design literals is matched by exactly its dedicated pattern id, and the cross-catalogue half by asserting the FY strings produce no term candidate.

design_cites.quote: Academic terms such as Spring 2025, AY 2024-25, and Michaelmas Term 2024 require dedicated patterns rather than generic parsing.
Date candidates should be identified with explicit regular expressions and then parsed without fuzzy matching.
Date extraction should be deliberately narrow.

rules: **The three design literals are required rows and cannot be removed**: `Spring 2025` (atp-season-year), `AY 2024-25` (atp-academic-year-ay), `Michaelmas Term 2024` (atp-uk-named-term). P6's Task 12 asserts them by pattern identity, not by value.

**A term candidate is a candidate, not a fact.** Every match still passes §3.7's ranked fill with injected minimum score and margin. The rows below that carry heavy false-friend load (season-year, standalone ranges) say so; none is pre-weighted, because weights are injected.

**A term hit alone activates nothing.** `Spring 2025` in a fashion lookbook must not open the Academic schema. As an activation signal (CONNECTION.md step 1) a term-pattern hit is never-alone: it supports activation only beside another independent academic signal (a course-code pattern with context, a floor context term, an academic gazetteer hit).

**Arithmetic validation is part of the pattern contract.** Rows flagged `validation: consecutive_year_two_digit` accept a match only when the trailing two digits equal the leading year plus one (modulo one hundred); `consecutive_year_full` requires the trailing four-digit year to be the leading year plus one. `AY 2024-27` matches the regex and is rejected by validation — check.py exercises both halves. This is a calendar identity, like catalogue 06's checksums — not a tunable threshold.
**No fuzzy parsing, ever.** `parse_exact` maps named groups to a value; there is no path from an unmatched string to a term, and no generic year regex exists in this file (a bare year is refused).
**No numbers as data.** Regex digits and quantifiers are pattern shape; the JSON carries no score, weight, window, or tolerance.

validation_rules.consecutive_year_two_digit: the digits after the separator must name the year after the leading four-digit year: a two-digit tail passes when it equals the leading year plus one modulo one hundred, a four-digit tail passes when it equals the leading year plus one. 2024-25 and 2024/2025 pass; 2024-05, 2024-27, 2024-24 fail.
validation_rules.consecutive_year_full: the four-digit year after the separator must equal the leading four-digit year plus one. 2024-2025 passes; 2022-2027 and 2024-2024 fail.
validation_rules.consecutive_year_two_digit_when_range: consecutive_year_two_digit applied only when the optional year-range group matched; a rangeless match (Sommersemester 2025, WiSe 2025) carries no range to validate and passes as a single-year term.
validation_rules.note: all three are calendar identities (an academic year spans two consecutive calendar years); none is a tunable number. They double as the ISO-date firewall: 2024-05 inside 2024-05-11 is already excluded by lookahead, and fails validation besides.

entries.rationale: The first design literal, generalized to the five season words US and UK institutions actually print (Fall and Autumn are the same term on different transcripts). Case-insensitive because filenames and OCR lowercase freely; the cost is prose noise ('in spring 2025 we planted'), which is real term-like usage anyway and is left to §3.7's zone weights and margin.
entries.quote: Academic terms such as Spring 2025, AY 2024-25, and Michaelmas Term 2024 require dedicated patterns rather than generic parsing.
matches_but_must_not_conclude: Salesforce Spring 2025 release (software release naming — Salesforce ships Spring/Summer/Winter releases)
entries.source: software-release false friend verified against Salesforce Spring '25 release announcements (RESEARCH.md)

entries.pattern_label: AY + year range, hyphen or en-dash (AY 2024-25)
entries.rationale: The second design literal. Case-sensitive: lowercase `ay` is an English word and an ending ('may', 'day'); the word boundary already refuses `MAY 2024-25` and case-sensitivity refuses standalone 'ay 2024-25'. The separator class accepts both the hyphen and the en-dash because both appear in real registrar text (the dispatch names the en-dash/hyphen fork; both are one entry here, with the separator preserved in `raw value`).
entries.quote: Academic terms such as Spring 2025, AY 2024-25, and Michaelmas Term 2024 require dedicated patterns rather than generic parsing.
entries.source: registrar usage; consecutive-year identity is the calendar itself

entries.rationale: The full-width form of the same designator, common in formal documents. Separate row so parse_exact has an unambiguous group layout; same validation discipline.

entries.pattern_label: named UK term + Term + year (Michaelmas Term 2024)
entries.rationale: The third design literal, generalized to the real sibling names: Oxford runs Michaelmas/Hilary/Trinity, Cambridge runs Michaelmas/Lent/Easter, Durham runs Michaelmas/Epiphany/Easter. The word `Term` is required in this row: without it, Easter and Lent are holidays and Michaelmas is a feast day (29 September). The no-`Term` variant is an uncertain row.
entries.quote: Academic terms such as Spring 2025, AY 2024-25, and Michaelmas Term 2024 require dedicated patterns rather than generic parsing.
matches_but_must_not_conclude: the English legal year uses the same four term names (Hilary, Easter, Trinity, Michaelmas) for court sittings — 'Michaelmas Term 2024' in a barrister's listing is a legal term, not coursework; domain evidence and margin decide
entries.source: Oxford/Cambridge/Durham term naming verified by web survey 2026-08-22 (RESEARCH.md); legal-year collision verified against the UK judiciary's own term listing in the same survey

entries.rationale: The US quarter system (Stanford, UChicago, UW, and others) writes terms as season + Quarter. The dispatch names Winter quarter explicitly. Reversed order ('2025 Winter Quarter') is an uncertain row.
entries.design_cite: 00 §3.10 (dedicated-pattern discipline applied to a researched system)

entries.rationale: Semester 1 / Semester 2 is the standard Australian and New Zealand transcript naming (verified survey: ANU calendars and general Australian academic-calendar guides — RESEARCH.md), also common across Asia. The year is required in this row: `Semester 1` alone names no year and cannot be a dated term value (uncertain row). `Semester 3` (some trimester systems) is an uncertain row, not authored.
entries.design_cite: 00 §3.10 (dedicated-pattern discipline applied to a researched system)
entries.source: ANU academic calendars; Australian academic-calendar guides (RESEARCH.md)

entries.rationale: German universities divide the year into Wintersemester (October–March, written with a slash range because it spans two years) and Sommersemester (April–September, single year). Verified by survey (uni-assist glossary, TU Darmstadt semester dates — RESEARCH.md). The slash tail accepts two or four digits (2024/25 and 2024/2025 both occur); when a range is present the consecutive-year identity applies; a rangeless Wintersemester is still a valid transcript form.
entries.design_cite: 00 §3.10 (dedicated-pattern discipline applied to a researched system)
entries.source: uni-assist glossary; TU Darmstadt semester dates (RESEARCH.md)

entries.rationale: WiSe and SoSe are the standard German abbreviations (verified survey — RESEARCH.md: 'The academic year in Germany is divided into winter semester (WiSe) and summer semester (SoSe)'). Case-sensitive: lowercase `wise` and `sose` are ordinary words ('wise 2024 investors'). The bare `WS`/`SS` abbreviations are riskier — `SS 2025` collides with too much and `WS 2024` with workstation naming — so WS is a separate slash-requiring row and SS is refused.
entries.design_cite: 00 §3.10 (dedicated-pattern discipline applied to a researched system)

entries.rationale: The older WS abbreviation is only accepted with the full slash range, whose consecutive-year identity is the disambiguator; bare `WS 2024` could be anything and is not authored. `SS` (Sommersemester's older abbreviation) is refused outright — see refused.
entries.design_cite: 00 §3.10 (dedicated-pattern discipline applied to a researched system)

entries.pattern_label: year + 年度 (2024年度 — Japanese April-start academic/fiscal year)
entries.rationale: 年度 (nendo) marks Japan's April-to-March year, used identically for the school year and the fiscal year (verified survey — RESEARCH.md). word_boundary is false by necessity: CJK characters are word characters to the regex engine, so `\b` cannot bound the suffix; the lookbehind refuses a longer digit run instead. The academic-vs-fiscal fork is the same one FY carries in Latin script: the string alone cannot say which, so this row is a candidate producer whose field routing (term vs a fiscal field) must come from surrounding evidence — see NEEDS-JOSEPH. Era-year forms (令和6年度) and 学期-based semester names are the uncertain CJK slot, not authored.
entries.design_cite: 00 §3.10 (dedicated-pattern discipline applied to a researched convention); 00 §2.7 names CJK support explicitly
matches_but_must_not_conclude: 事業年度 / corporate fiscal-year usage — a Japanese annual report writes the identical string for its fiscal year
entries.source: nendo definition and April-start convention verified by web survey 2026-08-22 (RESEARCH.md)

entries.rationale: The dispatch's en-dash-vs-hyphen research lands here: both separators, one row. Restricted to 20xx on purpose — 19xx standalone ranges in a personal corpus are overwhelmingly historical references, not the user's academic years (refused row). The trailing lookahead refuses ISO dates (`2024-05-11` never yields `2024-05`), and the consecutive-year identity refuses year-month strings besides. The leading lookbehind refuses any word character, so a letter-attached range never fires: `v2024-25` and `FY2024-25` produce nothing from this row. Evaluated last: a span claimed by the AY/WS rows here or by 12/04's designator families (`FY 2024-25`) is never offered here.
entries.design_cite: 00 §3.10 (the AY literal's range, without its designator)
examples_false: AY 2024-25 (claimed by the AY row under evaluation_order)
matches_but_must_not_conclude: sports seasons — the NBA 2024-25 season passes the consecutive-year identity; zone weights, co-occurring academic evidence, and margin must carry it

entries.rationale: The full form of the previous row, with the same discipline: word-character lookbehind (no letter-attached ranges) and range-continuation lookahead (`2024-2025-26` yields nothing — a three-part range is a page span or an outline number, not an academic year). The consecutive-year identity is what separates an academic year from a grant period (2022-2027), a war (1914-1918 — also 19xx-excluded), or a page range that happens to contain year-shaped numbers.
entries.design_cite: 00 §3.10 (the AY literal's range, without its designator)
matches_but_must_not_conclude: consecutive-year sports seasons and two-year budget cycles pass the identity; margin and context decide

refused.rationale: The dispatch asked for FY research; the answer is that FY is a fiscal designator, not an academic term. Universities use FY for budgets, not transcripts. The pattern is authored in catalogue 12/04 as the fiscal-year family, whose candidate targets the Finance domain's tax-year field — it must never fill `term`. Listed here so nobody re-adds it as a term row.
refused.design_cite: 00 §3.11 (Finance's field list carries tax year; Academic's carries term)

refused.rationale: A business reporting quarter, never an academic term. Catalogue 06's check already treats `Q3 2024` as a date leak; this file agrees from the other side. Academic quarters are written with season words (atp-quarter-year).

refused.pattern_label: a season word with no year
refused.rationale: `Spring` alone is a mattress, a coil, a verb, a water source, and a Java framework. Without a year it names no term value and must produce no candidate.

Genuinely used in older German documents, but the collision surface (abbreviations, model names, the historical reading) is disqualifying and SoSe covers the modern usage. A user with a German corpus who needs it can inject it deliberately.

In a personal corpus a standalone 19xx range is a historical reference (wars, biographies, citations) far more often than the user's own academic year. The AY-prefixed rows keep (19|20) because the designator disambiguates; the standalone rows do not.

refused.pattern: (an ISO date is never a term)
refused.pattern_label: calendar dates offered to the term field
refused.rationale: A term is a named academic period, not a day. Calendar-date families live in catalogue 12/04 and target date fields; no date family may fill `term`, and the lookahead + consecutive-year identity on the range rows keep ISO fragments out mechanically.

uncertain.pattern_label: UK named terms without the word Term (Michaelmas 2024)
uncertain.rationale: Real usage drops `Term` ('Michaelmas 2024 timetable'), but Michaelmas is also a feast day and dropping the anchor invites the religious-calendar reading; Lent and Easter without `Term` are firmly holidays and could never join. Needs corpus evidence for the three safer names.
Live student/staff shorthand, but MT is Mountain Time, LT a lieutenant, ET a film. Two letters + two digits is too little signal to author without corpus evidence and a context requirement.

Real academic usage ('Class of ’25') and the exact form of Salesforce's release naming (Spring '25 — verified). Straight vs curly apostrophe doubles the pattern surface and the software false friend is at its worst here. Deferred to corpus evidence.
Occurs in some registrar exports. Low risk but unverified frequency; add on evidence.

UNSW runs T1/T2/T3; some systems use Semester 3 for summer; trimester naming varies. T1/T2/T3 + year is dangerously short (T1 is a network line, T2 a film). Needs per-institution evidence before authoring.

uncertain.pattern_label: Term 1–6 + year (UK schools run six terms, AU four)
uncertain.rationale: School (not university) naming, so it depends on whose corpus this is; 'term' also carries contract/lease senses ('lease term 1 2025' is lexically close). Plausible, unauthored pending corpus evidence.

uncertain.pattern_label: 学期 / 學期 / 학기 semester forms, era years (令和6年度)
uncertain.rationale: 春学期 / 秋学期 (spring/fall semester), 第一学期 (first semester), 제1학기 / 1학기 (Korean), and Japanese era-year forms (令和6年度, which needs era arithmetic to normalize) are real conventions this file cannot author honestly without native review and a corpus. Recorded as the named slot `cjk_term_patterns_slot`; only the 年度 row above was confident enough to author.
Some institutions write AY 2024 for the year starting 2024. Rangeless, so the consecutive-year identity cannot vouch for it; the AY designator alone is decent signal. Deferred to corpus evidence.

acceptance_fixtures: tests/eval/fixtures/adversarial/A03.json — `MA 02139` and `XPS 13` must produce no term fact from any row here (no row matches either)
P6 SPEC Done-means 10 — `v2024`, a build number, and a ZIP code produce no date fact; `Spring 2025`, `AY 2024-25`, and `Michaelmas Term 2024` each produce exactly one term fact
sourcing_note: Oxford (Michaelmas/Hilary/Trinity), Cambridge (Michaelmas/Lent/Easter), Durham's Epiphany term, the English legal year's identical term names, German Wintersemester/Sommersemester with WiSe/SoSe abbreviations, Australian Semester 1/2 naming, Japanese 年度, and the Salesforce seasonal-release false friend were all verified by web survey on 2026-08-22; URLs in RESEARCH.md. The US quarter system row rests on general knowledge recorded in RESEARCH.md's anchor list. Everything unverified is in uncertain, not entries.
